chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from 'Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Hammad, from Hariz, from one who informed him, from Abu 'Abdillah عليه السلام, who said:

Whoever drives a sacrificial animal voluntarily and it becomes incapacitated, then nothing is due upon him. He should slaughter it, take the sandal of taqlid, dip it in the blood, and strike with it the side of its hump, and no replacement is due upon him. But whatever is from the compensation for hunting or a vow, and it becomes incapacitated, he should do the like of that, and a replacement is due upon him. And everything that, once it has entered the Haram, becomes incapacitated, then no replacement is due upon its owner, whether it was voluntary or otherwise.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: This report does not contradict what we have previously presented, namely that a replacement is due whether it reached its destination or did not reach it, because this is to be understood as referring to when it becomes incapacitated in a way short of death, such as a fracture, illness, or the like. In that case, as we have described, it suffices on behalf of its owner. This is indicated by that.

key_terms.الْبَدَلُ: the replacement animal or substitute obligation due
key_terms.تَطَوُّعًا: as a voluntary offering, not one made obligatory by vow or penalty
key_terms.جَزَاءِ صَيْدٍ: an offering due as compensation for hunting while in ihram
key_terms.عَطِبَ: became incapacitated, damaged, or perished before completion
key_terms.نَذْرٍ: a vowed obligation made binding upon oneself
key_terms.نَعْلَ التَّقْلِيدِ: the sandal used as a mark to identify the sacrificial animal
key_terms.هَدْيًا: a sacrificial animal driven for offering in hajj

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if a sacrificial animal for hajj becomes incapacitated before reaching its destination?
ai.summary: This hadith discusses the rulings of sacrificial animals designated for hajj when they become incapacitated before reaching their place of sacrifice. It distinguishes between voluntary offerings, compensatory offerings, and vowed offerings, and it also records Shaykh al-Tusi's reconciliation of this report with other narrations by interpreting the damage as something short of death.
